title: The more laws
hookLine: the more prohibitions, the poorer the people; I do nothing and they change themselves (Tao Te Ching 57)

cards: Taped to the fridge in a shared apartment: label your food. Below it, in different handwriting: and wash your dishes the same day. Below that: no dishes in the sink overnight, this means you.
Then: who used my oat milk. By the end of the semester the fridge door is a wall of notes, the sink is full, and nobody speaks to anybody in the kitchen. More rules went up, and the place got worse.
Chapter fifty-seven of the Tao Te Ching saw this pattern long before refrigerators, and wrote it at the size of a whole kingdom.

teach.h: THE WORLD IS WON BY NOT MEDDLING.
teach.b: First, three ways to hold power. A state is governed by what's correct, the chapter says, and a war is fought with surprise. But the world itself is won by not meddling.
The more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people become. The more sharp tools people have, the more disorder in the land. The more cleverness, the more strange contraptions.
The more laws are put on display, the more thieves and robbers appear. It's a run of mores, and each one backfires. Third, the sage's answer.
In James Legge's translation, a sage has said: "I will do nothing (of purpose), and the people will be transformed of themselves."
The chapter goes on in the same rhythm: the sage loves stillness, and the people settle themselves. The sage doesn't meddle, and they prosper.

teach.h: THE SAGE DOES NOTHING; THEY CHANGE.
teach.b: The sage wants nothing, and they return to simplicity.
Readers take this more than one way. Some read it as political advice: govern lightly. Others read it closer to home, about anyone with a little authority over anyone else.
A parent with a rule for everything. A manager who answers every mistake with a new policy. A partner keeping a quiet rulebook the other person never saw.
The chapter isn't saying no one should ever set a limit. Read this way, it raises a sharper question: does this rule make things better, or does it just make you feel in control?

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter fifty-seven both as advice to rulers to govern lightly and as a personal teaching for anyone with authority: meddle less, and let people settle themselves.

o: piling on rules that make things worse, not better
an old list of laws the sage once wrote down
a game where the players invent rules as they go

s: chapter fifty-seven says more laws make fewer thieves
it says the more laws are put on display, the more thieves and robbers appear.
the chapter says a war is fought with surprise
a state by what's correct, a war by surprise, and the world won by not meddling.
the chapter forbids anyone ever setting a limit
it lists rules that backfire and pictures a sage who meddles less; it doesn't ban all limits.

games.q: you govern a restless land. thefts are up and people are poor. what does chapter fifty-seven's sage do?
o: do less, keep still, and let people settle.
games.why: the sage does nothing of purpose and loves stillness, and the people are transformed of themselves and grow settled and prosperous.

practice: Bring to mind the people you have some say over, at home, at work, on a team, and quietly list a few of the rules you keep for them, spoken or unspoken: how the towels get folded, when someone should text back.
Find one rule that's more about your comfort than their good, and picture a day without it. Notice what tightens, and what eases.

wordCard.voice: The more laws. Chapter fifty-seven: the more prohibitions, the poorer the people, and the more laws on display, the more thieves. The sage meddles less, and people change of themselves. Today's word.
